# Getting scribl onto other people's Android phones

This is the Android counterpart to the iOS Distribution page. scribl produces
three build outputs from one Expo codebase: the web export (hosted on
S3/CloudFront), the Android APK (this page), and the iOS build (see iOS
Distribution). This page covers the native Android output: what it is, how it is
generated, and how to hand it to testers.

## TL;DR / recommendation

Yes. On Android you really can hand someone a file. The build output is a
`.apk`, and a tester can install it directly by allowing "install from unknown
sources." No paid account, no per-device registration, no store review. For a
small tester/investor group, share the debug APK directly. To scale to a broad
audience with auto-updates, use Google Play internal/closed testing later.

This is the freedom iOS does not give you: Android does not gate install behind
a vendor signing service, so a self-signed debug APK runs on any phone whose
owner opts in.

## What the output is

- `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk` -- a self-contained,
  debug-signed Android package. This is the Android analog of an iOS `.ipa`, but
  unlike an `.ipa` it installs without Apple/Google involvement.
- App id: `com.hs2studio.scribl` (set as `android.package` in app.json).
- The `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` values are inlined into the JS bundle AT BUILD TIME, so the
  backend URL the app talks to is fixed when the APK is built. Changing it means
  rebuilding.

## How the APK is generated

scribl is an Expo SDK 56 managed app (RN 0.85.3, Skia + Reanimated + worklets).
Plain Expo Go cannot load those native modules, so a compiled build is required.
The android-native-build agent owns this flow. Toolchain: Android Studio (SDK +
JDK 21 + NDK).

```sh
# From vendor/mobileapp, with the Android SDK/JDK env set:
npx expo-doctor                         # surface version-alignment issues early
npx expo prebuild --platform android    # generate the native android/ project

# Build + install + launch on an emulator/device, backend baked in:
EXPO_PUBLIC_API_MODE=http \
EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=http://10.0.2.2:8787 \
npx expo run:android

# Or a standalone APK to hand out:
cd android && EXPO_PUBLIC_API_MODE=http \
  EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=http://10.0.2.2:8787 \
  ./gradlew assembleDebug
# -> android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
```

`android/` (like `ios/`) is gitignored by design: it is regenerated by prebuild
and never committed. The only committed change the native build needs is the
one-line `android.package` in app.json (mirrored on iOS by `ios.bundleIdentifier`).

## Distributing to testers

- **Hand them the file (simplest).** Send `app-debug.apk` by any channel (email,
  Drive, a download link). On the phone: Settings -> allow "install from unknown
  sources" for that app/browser, open the APK, tap Install. Done. Best for a
  small known group.
- **Google Play internal testing (scales).** Upload an AAB to the Play Console
  (25 USD one-time developer fee), add testers by email; they install via Play
  and get auto-updates. Use this when the tester list grows or you want update
  management. Heavier setup than handing over an APK.

## Backend connectivity for Android testers

The backend URL is baked into the APK at build time via `EXPO_PUBLIC_*`. Choose
it for the target:

- Android **emulator** reaches a backend on the host at `10.0.2.2` (the
  emulator's alias for the host loopback), for example
  `http://10.0.2.2:8787`. This is the Android-specific convention; the iOS
  Simulator uses `localhost` instead.
- A **physical Android phone** on the same LAN uses the host's LAN IP, for
  example `http://192.168.68.52:8787`.
- A build handed to a **remote tester** cannot reach a backend on the dev
  laptop at all. It needs a publicly reachable backend URL baked in at build
  time. Treat the backend URL as a real per-audience build decision.

## Status

The Android APK build path is established and owned by the android-native-build
agent: `expo prebuild --platform android` plus a Gradle debug build produce
`app-debug.apk`, installable on an emulator or a physical phone. The NDK and any
version-alignment fixes (RN 0.85 / Skia / Reanimated) are handled inside that
agent's flow.

## Android vs iOS, in one line

Android: self-signed APK, side-load with one opt-in, free. iOS: every install is
signed through Apple, so there is no free hand-them-a-file path -- use TestFlight
(see iOS Distribution). Same Expo codebase, same `com.hs2studio.scribl` id, two
very different distribution stories.
